'''Naomi McClure-Griffiths''' {{Post-nominals|country=AUS|FAA}} (born July 11, 1975) is an American-born Australian [[astrophysicist]] and [[radio astronomer]]. She is the first Chief Scientist of the [[Square Kilometre Array Observatory]]<ref name="SKAO Chief Scientist">{{cite news|title=Prof. Naomi McClure-Griffiths becomes SKAO's first chief scientist|url=https://www.skao.int/en/news/655/first-skao-chief-scientist|access-date=3 June 2026}}</ref>. In 2004, McClure-Griffiths discovered a new [[spiral arm]] in the [[Milky Way]] galaxy. She was awarded the [[Prime Minister's Prizes for Science|Prime Minister's Malcolm McIntosh Prize for Physical Scientist]] in 2006 and in 2015 was honored for her research in physics by receipt of the [[Pawsey Medal]] from the [[Australian Academy of Science]]. This was followed by an [[Australian Laureate Fellowship]] in 2021,<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-06-23|title=2021 Laureate Profile: Professor Naomi McClure-Griffiths|url=https://www.arc.gov.au/news-publications/media/funding-announcement-kits/australian-laureate-fellowships-2021/2021-laureate-profile-professor-naomi-mcclure-griffiths|access-date=2021-11-04|website=Australian Research Council|language=en}}</ref> while in 2022 she was elected a Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science]].<ref name="Australian_Academy_of_Science2022-1">{{Cite web |date=2022-05-26 |title=Academy announces 2022 Fellows for outstanding contributions to science |url=https://www.science.org.au/news-and-events/news-and-media-releases/two-firsts-academy-announces-2022-fellows |access-date=2022-05-25 |website=Australian Academy of Science |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Naomi Melissa McClure-Griffiths was born on July 11, 1975, in [[Atlanta]] [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]].<ref name=CV>{{cite web|title=Curriculum Vitae: Naomi McClure-Griffiths|url=http://www.atnf.csiro.au/people/nmcclure/cv.html~|publisher=CSIRO Australia Telescope National Facility|access-date=24 November 2015|location=Epping, New South Wales, Australia|date=2006}}</ref> She entered [[Oberlin College]] in 1993 where she studied both French and physics and then in 1997 entered the [[University of Minnesota]] to study astrophysics. During her PhD, she participated in the [[International Galactic Plane Survey]], leading the Southern Galactic Plane Survey to map the hydrogen gas in the [[Milky Way]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McClure‐Griffiths |first=N. M. |last2=Dickey |first2=John M. |last3=Gaensler |first3=B. M. |last4=Green |first4=A. J. |last5=Haverkorn |first5=Marijke |last6=Strasser |first6=S. |date=June 2005 |title=The Southern Galactic Plane Survey: H I Observations and Analysis |url= |journal=The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series |volume=158 |issue=2 |pages=178–187 |doi=10.1086/430114 |issn=0067-0049}}</ref>

==Career==
In 2001, she relocated permanently to Australia taking up a post doctoral fellowship at the Australia Telescope National Facility as a [[CSIRO]] Bolton Fellow.<ref name="PM's prize">{{cite news|title=2006 Malcolm McIntosh Prize for Physical Scientist of the Year|url=http://science.gov.au/community/PrimeMinistersPrizesforScience/Recipients/2006/Pages/Dr-Naomi-McClure-Griffiths.aspx|access-date=24 November 2015|publisher=Commonwealth of Australia Department of Industry, Innovation and Science|date=2006|location=Canberra, Australia}}</ref> During her fellowship, McClure-Griffiths studied the movement of interstellar gases and how explosions of stars create bubbles or shells which push the gasses out of the galaxy. In their movement, chimneys of empty space may be created, two of which were discovered by McClure-Griffiths. One of the chimneys she discovered is the only known chimney to "extend through the top and bottom of the galactic plane". Then in 2004, she discovered a new [[spiral arm]]<ref name="PM's prize" /> during her senior postdoctoral position.<ref name="speech">{{cite web|title = Dr Naomi McClure-Griffiths – speech|url = https://grants.innovation.gov.au/SCOPE/pages/doc.aspx?name=WISE_McClureGriffiths.htm|publisher = Government of Australia Department of Industry|access-date = 24 November 2015|location = Canberra, Australia|date = 25 June 2014|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151222162913/https://grants.innovation.gov.au/SCOPE/pages/doc.aspx?name=WISE_McClureGriffiths.htm|archive-date = 22 December 2015}}</ref> The new arm was shown on previous mappings but never identified nor given a name. McCure-Griffiths created a computer model to confirm its existence which was confirmed by her team.<ref name="2004 arm">{{cite news|title=Milky Way spiral gets an extra arm|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn4959-milky-way-spiral-gets-an-extra-arm/|access-date=24 November 2015|publisher=[[New Scientist]]|date=9 May 2004|location=London, UK}}</ref> 

In 2006, Naomi McClure-Griffiths was honored with the Malcolm McIntosh Prize for Physical Scientist of the year<ref name="Malcolm McIntosh Prize">{{cite news|title=Dr Naomi McClure-Griffiths, Astrophysicist|url=http://www.abc.net.au/catalyst/stories/s1982932.htm|access-date=24 November 2015|publisher=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=19 July 2007|location=Sydney, Australia}}</ref> one of the annual prizes awarded as the Prime Minister's Prizes for Science.<ref name="2006 Recipients">{{cite web|title=2006 Recipients|url=http://science.gov.au/community/PrimeMinistersPrizesforScience/Recipients/2006/Pages/default.aspx|publisher=Australian Government Department of Industry, Innovation and Science|access-date=24 November 2015|location=Canberra, Australia|date=2006}}</ref> As Principal Investigator she initiated the Galactic All Sky Survey that same year<ref name="PM's prize" /><ref name="Malcolm McIntosh Prize" /> and then in 2007, she was the recipient of the Powerhouse Wizard Award from the [[Powerhouse Museum]] at the [[Sydney Observatory]].<ref name="Sydney Observatory">{{cite web|last1=Lomb|first1=Nick|title=Astrophysicist announced as the 2007 Powerhouse Wizard|url=http://www.sydneyobservatory.com.au/2007/astrophysicist-announced-as-the-2007-powerhouse-wizard/|access-date=24 November 2015|publisher=Sydney Observatory|date=13 November 2007|location=Sydney, Australia}}</ref> McClure-Griffiths' team took part in the international effort to complete the mapping of the Milky Way's magnetic fields in 2011.<ref name=mapping>{{cite news|title=Milky Way's Magnetic Fields Mapped with Highest Precision|url=http://www.spacedaily.com/reports/Milky_Way_Magnetic_Fields_Mapped_with_Highest_Precision_999.html|access-date=24 November 2015|publisher=Space Daily|date=12 December 2011|location=Munich, Germany}}</ref> In 2015, she left CSIRO and joined the Australian National University as a professor conducting her research from the [[Mount Stromlo Observatory]].<ref name="new job">{{cite web|title=ANU Spaces – Naomi McClure-Griffiths|work=ANU |url=http://www.anu.edu.au/news/all-news/anu-spaces-%E2%80%93-naomi-mcclure-griffiths|publisher=[[Australian National University]]|access-date=24 November 2015|location=Canberra, Australia|date=23 February 2015}}</ref> That same year, her work in physics was recognized by receipt of the Pawsey Medal from the [[Australian Academy of Science]].<ref name=Pawsey>{{cite web|title=2015 Honorific awards for scientific excellence|url=https://www.science.org.au/2015-honorific-awards-scientific-excellence#17|publisher=[[Australian Academy of Science]]|access-date=24 November 2015|location=Canberra, Australia|date=2015}}</ref> McClure-Griffiths was elected a Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science]] in 2022 for her contributions to our understanding of the atomic hydrogen gas distribution in our [[Milky Way]] and the [[Magellanic Clouds]] through observational surveys with Australian radio telescopes. <ref name="Australian_Academy_of_Science2022-1" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-06-01 |title=Naomi McClure-Griffiths elected to Australian Academy of Science |url=https://www.atnf.csiro.au/daily-picture/2022/06/01/naomi-mcclure-griffiths-elected-to-australian-academy-of-science/ |access-date=2026-11-09 |website=Australia Telescope National Facility |language=en-AU}}</ref> 

McClure-Griffiths was appointed the first Chief Scientist of the [[Square Kilometre Array Observatory]] in July 2025.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}}
